questions.question: Assertion (A): The algebraic sum of deviations of a set of observations from their mean is always zero.\nReason (R): The arithmetic mean represents the center of gravity of the distribution, balancing positive and negative deviations.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: sum[fi * (xi - x̄)] = sum(fi*xi) - x̄*sum(fi) = 0. Conceptually, the arithmetic mean is the balance point (center of gravity) where total positive deviations exactly cancel total negative deviations. Both statements are true and (R) correctly explains (A).
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics, Chapter 13 Statistics, Section 13.2

questions.question: Assertion (A): If the median of a distribution is 20 and mean is 22.5, then the mode is 15.\nReason (R): The empirical relationship between central tendencies is Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Using Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean: Mode = 3(20) - 2(22.5) = 60 - 45 = 15. Hence Assertion (A) is true, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains (A).
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics, Chapter 13 Statistics, Section 13.4

questions.question: Assertion (A): In a frequency distribution, the modal class is always the class interval with the highest frequency.\nReason (R): Mode is the value among the observations which occurs most frequently.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: By definition, mode is the observation with maximum frequency. For grouped data, the interval containing this maximum concentration is the modal class. Both are true and (R) explains (A).

questions.question: Assertion (A): The median of grouped data can be determined graphically as the x-coordinate of the intersection point of less than and more than ogives.\nReason (R): At the point of intersection of both ogives, the cumulative frequency equals N/2.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The less than ogive rises to N while the more than ogive falls from N. They intersect exactly at the height y = N/2, where the corresponding x value is the median. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).

questions.question: Assertion (A): When calculating the mean of grouped data, it is assumed that the frequency of each class is centered at its class mark.\nReason (R): Class mark is calculated as (Upper limit - Lower limit) / 2.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is true (this is the fundamental assumption of grouped data mean). Reason (R) is FALSE because class mark is (Upper limit + Lower limit)/2, whereas (Upper limit - Lower limit) is the class size.

questions.question: Assertion (A): If 5 is added to each observation of a data set with mean 20, the new mean becomes 25.\nReason (R): If a constant 'c' is added to each observation, the mean increases by 'c'.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: New mean = sum(xi + c)/n = sum(xi)/n + n*c/n = x̄ + c. Adding 5 to each observation increases the mean from 20 to 25. Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics, Chapter 13 Statistics, Section 13.2

questions.question: Assertion (A): Before finding the mode of grouped data with discontinuous class intervals (e.g. 1-10, 11-20), the intervals must be made continuous.\nReason (R): The formula for mode assumes continuous boundaries so that the class limit 'l' exactly touches the preceding interval.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The formula for mode Mode = l + [(f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)] * h requires continuous class limits, otherwise there is an unrepresented gap of 1 unit between classes. Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) explains (A).

questions.question: Assertion (A): The mean obtained by the direct method, assumed mean method, and step-deviation method is always identically the same.\nReason (R): Step-deviation and assumed mean methods are algebraic simplifications of the direct method, introducing no mathematical approximation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: All three methods are mathematically exact algebraic identities: x̄ = a + h * [sum(fi * ui)/sum(fi)] = a + sum(fi * di)/sum(fi) = sum(fi * xi)/sum(fi). They yield identical numerical answers. Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) explains (A).

questions.question: Assertion (A): For highly skewed income distributions with billionaires and low-wage earners, median is preferred over mean as the measure of central tendency.\nReason (R): Unlike the mean, the median is not disproportionately distorted by extreme extreme outlier values.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The median divides the ordered data in half and depends only on positional ranking, making it robust against extreme outliers. The mean incorporates the magnitude of every observation and is pulled strongly toward extremes. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).

questions.question: Assertion (A): If all classes in a frequency distribution have the exact same frequency, the distribution has no unique mode.\nReason (R): Mode requires one class to have a higher frequency than its neighboring classes.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: If every class has the same frequency, no single value or interval occurs more frequently than any other; hence the distribution is uniform and has no mode. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).
